CMS Stops $1.6 Billion in Fraudulent Medicare Lab Payments | Joe Chalfant, Townhall

The Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS) says it has stopped more than $1.6 billion in potentially improper Medicare laboratory payments since the start of the Trump Administration.

The agency said that it has slashed fraud and improved Medicare program integrity. This includes $732 million in savings from the revocation of 157 fraudulent lab providers from the Medicare program.

“When laboratories bill Medicare for tests they never performed, it drains the Medicare Trust Fund and diverts resources away from beneficiaries who need them,” said CMS Administrator Dr. Mehmet Oz. “That's why, under the leadership of the White House Anti-Fraud Task Force, CMS has built a technology-powered fraud prevention operation to root out scammers all across our health care system, from laboratory testing and hospice care to medical equipment and autism therapy. We won't stop until we've restored program integrity and ensured that fraudsters have nowhere left to hide.”

The $1.6 billion in enforcement actions taken by CMS include the following:

- Savings of $732 million from 157 fraudulent providers revoked from the Medicare program;

- Over $500 million in potentially fraudulent payments halted from 185 payment suspensions from CMS’ investigation of 600 labs;

- More than $276 million recouped from 442 identified overpayments already paid out to suspect labs; and

- $127 million in potentially fraudulent payments prevented as the result of 85 law enforcement referrals from a CMS contractor.

The savings in fraudulent payments were the result of CMS’ use of advanced analytics, including Artificial Intelligence and machine-learning models, to mine Medicare fee-for-service claims, looking for unusual billing patterns and other indicators of potential fraud, waste, or abuse.

AI can help identify potential laboratory fraud by learning what normal billing and laboratory activity looks like and flagging unusual combinations of testing, results, billing, documentation, and relationships that may indicate manipulation or fraudulent activity.

When these analytics identify high-risk billing patterns, CMS can use that information to automatically flag claims for further review and, when appropriate, hold, reject, or deny claims before any Medicare funds are released.

CMS has targeted several types of lab fraud, including billing for medically unnecessary services to beneficiaries with no established relationship with the ordering provider, as well as labs billing for services that were not rendered or for up-coded services. These fraudulent billing patterns can occur across a range of laboratory services including pathogen detection, high-complexity drug tests, and genetic testing.

Examples of fraudulent laboratory activity flagged by CMS:

- One individual who owned a consulting company enrolled 14 labs in Medicare fee-for-service and billed more than $24 million for services that could not have been rendered because none of the labs were found to be operational. CMS suspensions are currently holding $12 million―half of the labs’ total amount paid. CMS has recouped an additional $7 million in fraudulent payments from these entities and coordinated action has resulted in the revocation of the Medicare enrollments of 11 of the 14, while investigations continue for the remaining three.

- A Texas lab suspected of billing for services not rendered began billing at the end of February 2026 and received minimal payment before CMS detected the suspicious activity. The agency denied $1.2 million of the laboratory’s claims before the lab shifted billing practices in early April in an attempt to circumvent CMS controls. CMS analysts continued monitoring the lab, and a swift payment suspension prevented more than $150,000 in additional suspect payments. The provider was subsequently revoked that same month.

- Another Texas lab suspected of billing for services not rendered began billing in earnest in May 2026, following two days of test claim submissions in January and March 2026. CMS denied $1.9 million of the laboratory’s claims, while a payment suspension captured an additional $1.7 million. The provider is under CMS review for revocation.

Under the Trump Administration, CMS Medicare fraud prevention efforts have resulted in a record-shattering $42 billion in savings in Fiscal Year 2025 alone. So far in 2026, CMS has identified $1.8 billion in Medicare overpayments through medical review, collected $378 million in overpayments from post-payment reviews, and suspended more than $539 million in suspected fraudulent Medicare payments.

Since January 1, 2026, the CMS Fraud Defense Operations Center has accounted for more than $371 million in Medicare suspended payments involving 267 providers and suppliers including:

- More than $226 million for suspect durable medical equipment billing;

- More than $53 million to suspect providers/suppliers billing for skin substitutes; and

- More than $23 million to suspect hospice providers.

1.   The Program Layer

Most of these schemes sit on Medicaid home health, personal care assistance, or behavioral health reimbursement.

These programs have three properties that make them exploitable:

• Services are hard to verify physically
• Payments are volume based, not outcome based
• Oversight is post-payment, not pre-approval

The building with “14 companies” is a feature.

Each entity is:

• A separate LLC or nonprofit
• Registered to the same address
• Sharing staff, billing infrastructure, and often patients
• Legally distinct on paper

Why this matters:

When one entity gets flagged, the others keep billing.
When audits start, assets are already moved.
When licenses are revoked, new ones appear.

This is redundancy for fraud, exactly like redundant servers.

3.  The Billing Engine

Here’s how money actually moves.
1. Enroll patients who technically qualify
2. Enroll caregivers who technically qualify
3. Bill for maximum allowable hours
4. Inflate service frequency
5. Duplicate or overlap care claims
6. Auto-submit claims in bulk

Nobody checks whether care actually happened in real time.

Audits happen months or years later, if at all.

By then:

• Money is gone
• Entities are dissolved
• Principals are shielded

4.   Why the Same Address Keeps Appearing

Regulators flag individuals.
Fraud adapts by flagging entities instead.

One address means:

• Centralized paperwork
• Shared compliance consultant
• One billing contractor
• One legal defense structure

It looks sloppy from the outside.
It’s actually optimized for scale.

5.   The Oversight Failure Nobody Talks About

The system relies on:

• Whistleblowers
• Random audits
• Paper verification

There is no physical verification loop.
No biometric check.
No real-time service confirmation.

So the honest providers drown in compliance while dishonest ones scale faster.

That’s why this persists.

6.   Why This Keeps Getting Framed Wrong

People argue morality.
They argue politics.
They argue culture.

That misses the point.

This fraud exists because:

• Payment systems reward volume
• Oversight is delayed
• Fragmentation prevents pattern detection
• Accountability is diffuse

If this were defense contracts or agricultural subsidies, it would look identical.

Same mechanics. Different label.

7.   The Brutal Truth

This is rational behavior inside a broken incentive system.

The state built a system that assumes good faith.
Bad actors found the edge cases.
Then professionalized them.

Once that happens, the fraud does not stop until:

• Payments pause
• Verification becomes real-time
• Or political cost exceeds inertia

None of those are currently true.

8.   Why It Feels So Infuriating

Because you’re watching:

• Taxes converted into paper claims
• Care reduced to spreadsheets
• Trust turned into arbitrage

And the system keeps paying because stopping would expose how much is already gone.

That’s the quiet part.

Bottom line

This is process abuse at scale.

And until the payment architecture changes, new actors will replace old ones as fast as licenses can be filed.

That’s the real truth.

Trump administration freezes $867M in California Medicaid funds over suspected fraud | Benjamin Brown, New York Post

The Trump administration announced Tuesday that it’s halting more than $867 million in federal Medicaid payments to the Golden State over suspected fraud — with one expert describing it as a “piece of cake” for scammers to cash in.

“We are not sending Medicaid dollars out the door until we have confidence that they are being spent lawfully and appropriately,” Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. said during a press conference Tuesday.

The scandal centers around California’s In-Home Supportive Services (IHSS), a Medicaid-funded program that pays caregivers — often a family member — to help elderly and disabled residents at home instead of moving into a facility.

Over the past two years, Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS) Administrator Mehmet Oz said California’s spending for in-home services was “twice the rate of the average of the rest of the entire nation.”

“If it smells like fraud, we’re not paying for it anymore,” he said, adding that CMS is deferring payments until California can “substantiate their claims from this past quarter audit.”

Roughly $199 million in Medicaid funding in Minnesota was also frozen as part of the action.

Oz said CMS flagged suspicious billing patterns, including providers who submitted claims more than a year after services were provided, billed four or more patients simultaneously or ranked among the top 2.5% of billers nationwide.

Haywood Talcove, CEO of LexisNexis Risk Solutions for Government and a nationally recognized fraud expert, told The California Post that taxpayers should be “outraged” over the alleged lack of oversight that he said enables widespread fraud in California.

“Anytime you have a program like this where it is self-reported, there is virtually no auditing, and no one gets caught, then the probability of fraud is very, very high,” he said, estimating that fraud accounts for roughly 20% of the IHSS program.

Talcove explained how fraudsters can exploit IHSS, describing the process as a “piece of cake.”

According to Talcove, the fraud scheme begins when someone submits an IHSS application claiming to need in-home care, then designates a caregiver and persuades a licensed healthcare professional to falsely certify their need for care in exchange for a “cut.”

“I’ll tell you that your fake person that doesn’t exist needs home healthcare, and guess what? You’re going to give me a little cut. That’s how it goes,” Talcove said, adding that the “state doesn’t have the technology, doesn’t have the people, and doesn’t have the systems to validate it.”

Talcove argued California lacks the staffing, technology and incentive to adequately verify the state’s more than 500,000 IHSS recipients.

“There’s no money that comes out of the state pocket,” he said. “The incentive structure — federally funded, state-administered — is a recipe for disaster.”

California Governor Gavin Newsom rejected the administration’s claims of rampant fraud, describing the decision to halt payments as “pure politics.”

“We take fraud seriously,” Newsom said. “We don’t politicize it like these guys.”

The governor claimed that Tuesday’s announcement was an attack on his potential successor Xavier Becerra, the Democratic candidate for governor and a former Health and Human Services chief under former President Biden.

Newsom also said his office has been actively cooperating with the Trump administration, pointing to communications in which information requested from California was already provided.

“California’s approach, which had been long approved by CMS, saves federal and state taxpayers money,” a spokesperson for Newsom’s office told The Post. “One year of in-home care saves state and federal taxpayers approximately $100,000 per person annually versus nursing facility care. A 2020 California State Auditor report found no program integrity concerns and recommended increasing reimbursement rates to grow the in-home care provider workforce and reduce reliance on costly institutional care.”

Talcove believes the only way to prevent future fraud and abuse is to issue block grants and give the money directly to the states, or have the program fully funded and administered at the federal level.

“You can’t arrest and prosecute your way out of this,” he said.

In May, the Trump administration withheld $1.3 billion in Medicaid funding from California over mounting concerns tied to the state’s hospice and home-health agencies — bringing the current total over $2 billion.

The funds will be frozen until California and Minnesota can substantiate their claims and while federal officers review “high-risk” Medicaid claims.

“They need to provide documentation that these payments are legitimate,” Kennedy said.

Does the state of Minnesota have to pay all valid Medicaid claims regardless if the federal government freezes reimbursement, and how long does the state have to pay those claims?

Minnesota remains legally responsible for paying valid Medicaid claims even if the federal government freezes reimbursement. The state must continue administering its Medicaid program, and that includes processing and paying claims that meet eligibility and documentation requirements. Federal law does not give states an option to pause payments simply because federal matching funds are delayed or withheld.

There is no federal rule that sets a specific time limit for how long Minnesota must keep paying during a freeze. The obligation continues as long as the state operates Medicaid and has appropriated funds available. 

Minnesota can use its general fund, special reserves, or emergency appropriations to cover the federal share during a freeze. Once those resources are exhausted, the state may need legislative action, payment delays, or service reductions to remain solvent.

In practice, Minnesota will keep paying claims until it no longer has the financial capacity to do so. State officials have already warned that a prolonged freeze could force significant operational changes, including delayed payments or suspended services, because the financial burden shifts entirely to the state.

The Same Closed System, and Only One Side Can’t Get Paid

The third April ruling and the parallel body of provider-side enforcement cases, read together, reveal what Congress has not been willing to name: it built a closed system whose enforcement gap falls entirely on physicians.

UnitedHealthcare v. NorthStar Anesthesia (E.D. Pa., April 28, 2026)

UnitedHealthcare sued NorthStar Anesthesia after an IDR arbitrator awarded payment on an anesthesia claim for a Medicaid patient. The No Surprises Act does not apply to Medicaid. NorthStar acknowledged the filing was an error. A data processor had selected the wrong plan type from a dropdown menu. UnitedHealthcare sought declaratory and injunctive relief framed as a state common law fraud claim, arguing federal jurisdiction because the claim required interpretation of the NSA.

Judge Kearney dismissed for lack of subject matter jurisdiction. Under the Grable/Gunn test, a state law claim only arises under federal law if a federal issue is necessarily raised, actually disputed, substantial, and resolvable without disrupting the congressional balance of federal and state responsibilities. UnitedHealthcare’s claim failed the first and third elements. There is no dispute that Medicaid claims are ineligible for NSA IDR. Whether NorthStar knew that and filed fraudulently anyway is a question of fact, not a pure question of federal law, and it does not raise a substantial federal issue. The court also noted that Congress had provided specific administrative remedies for exactly this type of jurisdictional error, including Technical Assistance guidance from HHS, Labor, and Treasury addressing IDR filings involving Medicare and Medicaid patients, which UnitedHealthcare had not used. The court declined to remedy what UnitedHealthcare called a broken system and directed it to Congress.

Advanced Vascular Associates v. Horizon Blue Cross Blue Shield (E.D. Pa., April 7, 2026)

Three weeks earlier in the same district, Judge Wolson dismissed a provider’s attempt to confirm unpaid IDR awards under Section 9 of the Federal Arbitration Act. The NSA does not authorize that form of judicial relief. His instruction: the remedy for a statute Congress designed inadequately is Congress, not the courts.

Guardian Flight v. Health Care Service Corp. (5th Cir., June 2025)

Guardian Flight and Med-Trans won IDR awards. The insurer did not pay them. They sued. The Northern District of Texas dismissed. The Fifth Circuit affirmed in June 2025: the NSA structures enforcement through administrative penalties, not private litigation. Providers who are not paid must file CMS complaints. The Supreme Court declined to hear the appeal in January 2026. The Eleventh Circuit reached the same conclusion in November 2025. The Second Circuit will hear argument in a related case in June 2026.

What the administrative remedy actually looks like in practice

The Fifth Circuit said the remedy is administrative. Let me describe what that pathway actually looks like for the physician standing at the end of it.

A physician wins an IDR award. The insurer does not pay within the statutory 30-day window. The physician files a complaint with HHS. That complaint is referred to the Department of Labor for investigation under ERISA, which governs private sector employer-sponsored plans. The DOL opens a formal investigation and confirms it is open. It also confirms that it cannot escalate or expedite individual complaints. It cannot provide a specific timeline for resolution. It is fielding a significant volume of complaints about the same insurer’s handling of IDR payments after determination, enough that individual updates are not possible and all of them will be addressed through a consolidated investigation with no defined endpoint. The physician’s award remains unpaid throughout.

The closing instruction from the agency to the physician waiting for payment: if you want to pursue this matter while the investigation continues, you should contact your attorney.

That referral completes the circle. The Fifth Circuit told physicians the remedy is administrative. The administrative agency is telling physicians the remedy is legal. The attorney that physician calls cannot bring a private federal claim to enforce the IDR award in most circuits because the Fifth Circuit foreclosed it in June 2025 and the Supreme Court declined to intervene in January 2026.

This is the inevitable problem in the system. A physician with a binding IDR award that an insurer is not paying has, in practice, a complaint in a queue with no timeline, no provisional remedy, no automatic interest accruing, and no judicial option in most jurisdictions. The agency responsible for enforcement is managing a volume of complaints about a single insurer’s non-payment behavior that exceeds its capacity to respond individually. That is a documented pattern of systemic non-compliance meeting a statutory enforcement architecture that was not built to handle it.

The insurer inconsistency, documented in court filings

Aetna argued in Connecticut that the NSA bars judicial enforcement of IDR awards. This argument arose in a case where air ambulance providers sought payment for awards the defendant was alleged to have systematically ignored in what court filings characterized as a “low pay, late pay, or no pay” scheme described as a widespread business practice. The same Aetna simultaneously argued in Florida that courts should have authority to review and undo IDR outcomes when Aetna was the one seeking vacatur. The Fifth Circuit agreed with Aetna’s Connecticut position in June 2025. The Florida court rejected Aetna’s Florida position in April 2026. Aetna’s fully litigated posture across two federal circuits is: courts cannot be used to make us pay, and courts should be used to let us avoid paying. One position survived through the circuit level. The other died at the district court.

The enforcement asymmetry Congress wrote into the statute

A physician who submits an ineligible IDR claim faces award denial, fraud exposure, and potential loss of process access. Those consequences exist in the statute and they are enforced. An insurer that does not pay a binding IDR award faces a complaint to an agency whose enforcement authority on this specific question is legally contested, whose investigative timeline is undefined, and whose volume of complaints on the same conduct has outpaced its capacity to respond. Congress created detailed compliance obligations for the weaker party and left the enforcement obligations of the stronger party deliberately vague.

That asymmetry is the current state of the law and it will remain the current state of the law until Congress identifies and corrects it.

U.S. Patient Records Were Accessible From India. Doctors and Patients Carry the Risk.

In healthcare, clinicians are taught that patient data protection is non-negotiable. One mistake can end a career. One chart left open can trigger discipline, fines, or worse.

But upstream, very different rules apply.

A recent investigation found that a major Medicaid contractor struggled to prevent live U.S. patient records from being accessed by offshore workers in India. These were not test environments or anonymized files. Employees described real systems, real patients, and repeated failed attempts to restrict access.

For clinicians, this creates an immediate imbalance.

Physicians are personally accountable for privacy violations they do not control. Documentation errors, access mistakes, or compliance lapses can lead to termination or licensure risk. Yet decisions to expose patient data are made far from the exam room, justified as “efficiency,” and insulated from the same consequences imposed on individual providers.

For institutions, the risk is far larger than most acknowledge.

Offshore access to protected health information carries substantial regulatory and contractual exposure. HIPAA penalties can reach millions of dollars per violation. State Medicaid contracts often include termination clauses, clawbacks, and liquidated damages. False Claims Act exposure can surface years later through audits or whistleblower actions, long after any short-term savings have been booked.

There are operational risks that receive far less scrutiny than clinical ones.

Offshoring models often involve high workforce turnover, layered subcontracting, and limited transparency into credential verification and access controls. Rapid churn increases insider risk and reduces auditability. These are not country-specific accusations. They are structural risks inherent to moving sensitive healthcare data outside the same enforcement and oversight frameworks used domestically.

There is also a quiet asymmetry in who bears the consequences.

Organizations that maintain strict data protections rarely see immediate financial reward. Instead, they may watch competitors cut costs by accepting risks they refuse to take. Enforcement is uneven. When it arrives, it is swift and devastating. Those who treated safeguards as flexible absorb fines, contract loss, and reputational damage that can threaten institutional survival. Those who did not take the risk remain standing.

For patients, the breach is often invisible until trust is gone.

Patients reasonably assume their medical information is handled under U.S. legal protections, by accountable parties, under enforceable standards. They are rarely informed when their data is accessed offshore, under different legal regimes. Even without a reported breach, that assumption, once broken, is difficult to restore.

This is not an isolated incident.

Healthcare systems routinely claim they lack funding for staffing, training, or expanded residency slots. At the same time, administrative and technical functions tied directly to patient data are offshored in the name of efficiency. Safeguards are described as robust, but treated as negotiable under financial pressure.

Healthcare is not interchangeable with other industries.

Patient data is not a commodity.
Efficiency is not neutral when it shifts risk onto clinicians, institutions, and patients who did not consent to carry it.
If offshore access to patient data continues without enforceable, auditable boundaries, a single regulatory action or contract finding can easily dwarf years of operational savings.

The lesson is simple.
Waiting for enforcement to force change is the most expensive way to learn

"Insurers inventing more roadblocks to claims, providers say
Healthcare providers say insurance companies are innovating new ways to make it harder to get paid.
Physicians, hospitals and other providers have always complained of low rates, delayed payments and the usual red tape. But rules insurers such as Blue Cross Blue Shield of Michigan, UnitedHealthcare and Elevance Health have recently announced may be a new battleground in the age-old fight between the two camps.
Health insurance companies justify utilization management and claims review as crucial to constraining healthcare spending and ensuring that patients receive appropriate care. They also maintain that many claims are turned down because of provider error and that clarifying what's required upfront makes the reimbursement process more efficient.
Whatever the case, providers and patients have grown increasingly frustrated with the health insurance industry, which has attracted political attention.
Nearly one in five patients had a claim denied within the previous year, according to a survey the health policy research organization KFF conducted in February and March 2023. Prior authorization denials have become more common over the past five years, 74% of physicians reported in an American Medical Association survey last June.
“I appeal absolutely everything, and everything is a fight,” said Julie Baak, practice manager at the Arthritis Center, an independent infusion clinic in Bridgeton, Missouri, outside St. Louis.
Relationships between insurers and providers are deeply strained. Rates and timely reimbursements have always been sticking points, but providers say health insurance companies are snarling them with restrictions, such as more stringent prior authorization requirements.
“There's this whole front accelerating between insurers and providers that is not really about rates. It's more about appeals and denials. Insurers would much rather say no to a provider than a patient,” said Katherine Hempstead, senior policy advisor at the Robert Wood Johnson Foundation, a philanthropy that finances health research.
Now, one insurer is testing a new tactic: Charging providers to appeal rejected claims.
Beginning in March, Blue Cross Blue Shield of Michigan will assess fees when providers appeal some commercial claims. If a state external review board rules in favor of Blue Cross twice, the insurer will bill providers for the administrative costs associated with defending itself. The nonprofit insurer introduced the policy in 2021 but has not invoked it. Independent reviewers upheld its denials in 85% of cases last year, Blue Cross Blue Shield of Michigan said in a statement.
“We hope enforcing this policy will reduce unnecessary appeals costs in the future,” Blue Cross Blue Shield of Michigan said.
UnitedHealthcare is tightening up access to some screenings by requiring more documentation.
The UnitedHealth Group subsidiary is rolling out the fourth and final phase of a new system for molecular pathology tests in March. Under this policy, hospitals must submit additional, non-billing codes for commercial claims for hundreds of such tests. In addition to the standard Current Procedural Terminology reimbursement codes, providers will have to include Z-codes — which describe patient health status — for procedures such as prenatal screenings, genetic counseling and cancer tests. Medicare has the same rules, a UnitedHealthcare spokesperson wrote in an email.
“The Z-code allows for faster and more accurate provider reimbursement with fewer follow-up requests for records or information, reducing appeals and resubmissions, leading to a more accurate and positive provider claims experience,” the UnitedHealthcare spokesperson wrote.
To the contrary, said Terrence Cunningham, director of administrative simplification policy at the American Hospital Association. This new process adds to providers' administrative burden, not reduces it, he said.
“This is an emerging trend. Plans are trying to engage in additional medical assessment, and control costs more. In this case, they’re doing this in a way that is not efficient and leads to significant administrative costs being thrust upon providers,” Cunningham said. Moreover, he said, UnitedHealthcare vowed two years ago to ease access to genetic testing by cutting back on prior authorization requirements. UnitedHealth Group CEO Andrew Witty made a similar promise last Thursday.
Quantifying administrative burden is essentially impossible, in part because there are little publicly available data about what health insurance companies do and how often they do it. Starting in 2027, insurers participating in Medicare, Medicaid and the exchanges will be required to disclose how often and why they deny claims.
In the meantime, policymakers and the public are left with anecdotal accounts from healthcare professionals such as Baak, which increasingly are disseminated on social media platforms such as X and TikTok. These posts are finding a sympathetic audience amid the furor that arose after UnitedHealthcare CEO Brian Thompson's murder last month.
That backlash against the insurance industry coincided with one major company backtracking on a new cost-saving effort after providers protested.
Elevance Health subsidiary Anthem Blue Cross Blue Shield had planned to cap reimbursements in Connecticut, New York and Missouri for surgical anesthesia by setting time limits. But a successful pressure campaign led by the American Society of Anesthesiologists, fueled by news coverage and social media outrage, led the company to reverse itself, citing “significant widespread misinformation.”
Loren Adler, associate director for the Brookings Institution Center on Health Policy, said the "completely out of proportion" frenzy against Anthem forced the company to change course even though its policy was misrepresented as a threat to turn off anesthesia in the middle of operations. “They got a bunch of random people on Twitter to get upset about it, and it was a snowball effect,” he said.
This presents providers with a playbook they can duplicate in the current environment, Adler said. “I assume every anesthesia group is going to be like, ‘Well, now we're going to really write this into the contract and make it crystal clear what you can do here.'” (emphasis added)

Every state has applied for $50B Trump administration rural health fund | Nathaniel Weixel, The Hill

All 50 states have submitted applications for their share of a $50 billion pot of money to transform rural health, Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services (CMS) Administrator Mehmet Oz said Thursday.

Wednesday was the deadline for states to submit a detailed application for the first tranche of the five-year fund created to help rural providers offset the cuts to Medicaid and other health programs contained in the tax cut law.

“Each proposal must outline how states intend to expand access, enhance quality, and improve outcomes for patients through sustainable, state-driven innovation,” the CMS said. Award decisions will be made by Dec. 31.

The fund was created under the One Big Beautiful Bill Act passed this summer as a backstop against the nearly $1 trillion the law slashed from Medicaid.

“This program moves us from a system that has too often failed rural America to one built on dignity, prevention, and sustainability. Every state with an approved application will receive funding so it can design what works best for its communities—and CMS will be there providing support every step of the way,” Oz said in a statement.

When applications opened in September, the CMS said it would consider individual state metrics as well as “applications that reflect the greatest potential for and scale of impact on the health of rural communities.”

Under the program, $25 billion will be allocated to all states equally, meaning each state with an approved application would receive the same amount regardless of the size of its rural population.

The other $25 billion will be awarded at the discretion of Oz, based on criteria including whether states have adopted Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr.’s “make America healthy again” policies.

The CMS has outlined several approved uses for the funds, which include prevention and chronic disease management; payments to health care providers; and hiring new workers with commitments to serve rural communities for a minimum of five years.

The law gives Oz broad discretion on what he can approve, and there is no specific requirement for states to direct funds to rural hospitals or the CMS to approve only funding for rural districts.

Application denials can’t be appealed, nor can any administration decision to withhold funds over compliance concerns.

The One Big Beautiful Bill Act cuts about $1 trillion from Medicaid, primarily through stringent work requirements as well as reductions to how states can fund their Medicaid programs through provider taxes and state-directed payments.

Rural hospitals rely heavily on Medicaid funding because many of the patients they care for are low income. But the Trump administration has noted that rural hospitals only account for 7 percent of overall Medicaid spending.

The Great Health Insurance Heist: How the ACA Transformed Insurers from Risk-Bearers into Rent-Seeking Landlords

The Affordable Care Act promised to make health insurance work for everyone. Instead, it handed insurers the keys to a trillion-dollar monopoly.

The numbers tell a story that few politicians want to acknowledge: America's largest health insurers have raked in more than $371 billion in profits since the Affordable Care Act became law. UnitedHealth Group alone accounts for 40 percent of that windfall, with annual profits skyrocketing nearly 400 percent. Meanwhile, the average American family now pays nearly $26,000 per year for health insurance premiums, a burden that has grown relentlessly even as insurers post record earnings.

This is not the story of a free market succeeding or failing. This is the story of how well-intentioned healthcare reform inadvertently created the perfect conditions for what economists call "rent-seeking," the practice of extracting wealth without creating value. The ACA didn't just regulate the insurance industry; it fundamentally transformed it from a risk-bearing business into something resembling a landlord operation, where companies collect ever-increasing rents on a captive market while competition withers away.

The Transformation: From Risk to Rent
Before the ACA, health insurance operated on a traditional risk model. Insurers priced policies based on their assessment of potential losses, competed on coverage and price, and bore the financial consequences of their underwriting decisions. The system had serious flaws, denial of coverage for pre-existing conditions, arbitrary benefit caps, and discriminatory pricing, but it contained genuine competitive dynamics and real financial risk for insurers.

The ACA's well-intentioned reforms inadvertently dismantled this risk structure. The Medical Loss Ratio (MLR) rule requires insurers to spend 80 percent of premium revenue on medical claims and quality improvement, keeping only 20 percent for administrative costs and profits. This sounds like consumer protection, but it created a perverse incentive: insurers now profit more when total healthcare spending increases, because their 20 percent slice grows larger alongside the pie.

"The MLR rule fundamentally changed the business model," explains one former insurance executive who requested anonymity. "Instead of trying to efficiently manage risk and costs, we learned it was more profitable to let costs rise and take our percentage. We became landlords collecting rent on every healthcare transaction."

The transformation becomes clear when examining insurer stock performance. Since ACA implementation in 2014, health insurance stocks have outperformed the S&P 500 by 106 percentage points. The weighted average of health insurer stock prices has risen 1,032 percent since the ACA's passage in 2010, more than four times the S&P 500's growth over the same period.

The Death of Competition
The ACA's regulatory framework didn't just change insurer incentives; it systematically eliminated competition. Today, 95 percent of commercial insurance markets and 97 percent of Medicare Advantage markets are "highly concentrated" according to federal antitrust guidelines. In 89 percent of metropolitan areas, at least one insurer controls 30 percent or more of the commercial market.

This concentration didn't happen by accident. The ACA's complex regulatory requirements created massive barriers to entry while its elimination of key competitive mechanisms removed the checks and balances that previously constrained insurer behavior.

Consider what the law eliminated: The risk corridor programs that were supposed to share losses between government and insurers were defunded in 2016, denying insurers over $12 billion in promised payments. But rather than creating genuine market discipline, this elimination simply triggered a wave of strategic bankruptcies and market exits that further consolidated the industry.

Colorado provides a stark example. The state has witnessed a devastating pattern of insurance company failures over the past decade: Colorado HealthOP collapsed owing over $111 million in unpaid claims, Friday Health Plans liquidated affecting 30,000 consumers, Bright Health exited after being fined $1 million for failing to pay providers, and Humana withdrew from the employer group market affecting 183,000 members. Each failure reduced competition and left remaining insurers with greater market power. Needless to say, shafting the doctors who are held hostage by these plans. 

"We're not seeing normal business failures," notes a healthcare economist who has studied market concentration. "These companies often fail right around December, after maximizing their MLR spending for the year. It suggests strategic timing rather than random business pressures."

The Government ATM
The ACA didn't just reduce competition; it opened a direct pipeline from the federal treasury to private insurers. In fiscal year 2023 alone, federal subsidies through ACA Medicaid expansion and exchange premium tax credits totaled $218 billion, nearly all of which flowed to private insurers.

The Medicaid expansion has been particularly lucrative. The federal government pays nearly the entire cost of expansion enrollees, and most are covered through private Medicaid managed care plans. Since states are using almost entirely federal dollars, they set very high payment rates to insurers. Medicaid spending on private insurers more than quadrupled in inflation-adjusted dollars from 2010 to 2021.

The two largest Medicaid managed care companies exemplify this windfall: Molina's stock price has increased more than 1,000 percent since 2013, while Centene's has risen over 425 percent. Their business model is straightforward: collect government payments for covering low-income Americans while using every available tool to minimize actual care delivery.

The CEO Jackpot
The transformation of health insurance from risk-bearing to rent-seeking has produced spectacular rewards for executives. The CEOs of 70 major healthcare companies have earned $9.8 billion collectively in the seven years since the ACA's passage, nearly 11 percent more money on average each year.

Joseph Zubretsky of Molina Healthcare exemplifies this trend. In 2022, he received $181 million in compensation, more than half the total earned by all seven major health insurance CEOs combined. Molina gets all its revenue from taxpayer-funded programs, primarily Medicaid, yet Zubretsky's pay package ranks among the largest ever for a health insurance executive.

The compensation structure reveals the industry's priorities. CEO pay packages don't incentivize controlling healthcare costs or improving patient outcomes. Instead, they reward revenue growth and stock price appreciation, metrics that benefit from higher healthcare spending and market consolidation.

"Health care inflation continues to blow away general economic inflation, and a big reason why is because health care executives are not paid to slow spending," noted an analysis by Axios. This misalignment of incentives is not accidental; it's the logical result of a system that rewards rent extraction over value creation.

The Prior Authorization Racket
With traditional competition eliminated and profits tied to total spending volume, insurers have perfected new mechanisms for extracting value without bearing risk. Prior authorization, the requirement that doctors get permission before providing care, has become their primary tool.

The statistics are staggering. Roughly three in four Medicare Advantage enrollees are now in plans requiring prior authorization, with physicians completing an average of 39 authorization requests per week. This represents a dramatic shift from rare usage for expensive procedures to routine deployment across nearly all medical decisions. I have written here earlier about getting prior authorization for 5 ml of antibiotic! 

The timing patterns reveal the strategic nature of this expansion. Prior authorization requests spike in December as insurers race to meet their MLR spending requirements while simultaneously creating administrative barriers that delay care into the following year. Nearly 90 percent of physicians report that prior authorization actually increases overall healthcare resource utilization by forcing patients into emergency care when treatments are delayed.

"It's a perfect system," explains a primary care physician in Denver. "They collect 80 percent of premiums for 'medical costs' that include all their prior authorization infrastructure, then use that same infrastructure to delay or deny care. They profit coming and going."

The End Game: Monopoly by Design
The ACA's fundamental error was assuming that regulation could substitute for competition while maintaining market discipline. Instead, the law created a system where market failure becomes self-reinforcing. Each wave of insurer exits increases concentration, which reduces competition, which enables higher prices, which creates larger profit margins, which attracts more consolidation.

Government Accountability Office analysis confirms this trajectory: the private insurance market became increasingly concentrated from 2011 to 2022, with the number of states where a single insurer controls 80 percent of the large group market doubling from six to twelve.

This concentration has real consequences beyond higher premiums. Research shows that hospital consolidation, encouraged by insurers' need for predictable networks, results in higher prices with little evidence of improved care quality. A 1 percent increase in healthcare prices caused by hospital mergers reduces wages and employment at non-healthcare firms by 0.4 percent.

The Premium Explosion Ahead
The system's contradictions are now reaching a breaking point. ACA marketplace insurers are requesting premium increases averaging 15 percent for 2026, the largest since 2018. More than a quarter of insurers are proposing increases of 20 percent or more. If enhanced premium tax credits expire at the end of 2025, premium payments for subsidized enrollees will increase by over 75 percent.

These increases aren't driven by random healthcare inflation. They reflect the systematic incentives created by the ACA's structure. Insurers cite rising medical costs, but their own behavior ensures those costs will continue rising. The MLR rule means they profit more when spending increases, while their market dominance ensures they face no competitive pressure to control costs.

"We're approaching the end game of this system," warns healthcare economists.  "When competition is eliminated and profits are guaranteed, there's no natural limit to price increases. We've created a machine for extracting wealth from American families."

A Different Path Forward
The tragedy of the ACA is not that it failed to achieve universal coverage, millions more Americans have insurance today. The tragedy is that it could have achieved those same goals while preserving competition and controlling costs but instead chose a path that enriched incumbent insurers at the expense of everyone else.

Real healthcare reform would require acknowledging that the current system is working exactly as designed, not to provide efficient healthcare, but to generate profits for a concentrated industry. It would mean rebuilding genuine competition, realigning incentives to reward value over volume, and recognizing that complex regulations often serve incumbent interests rather than consumer welfare.

Until then, American families will continue paying ever-higher premiums to fund an industry that has mastered the art of extracting maximum rent from a captive market. The ACA promised to make health insurance work for everyone. Instead, it made health insurance work perfectly, for insurance companies.

U.S. Patient Records Were Accessible From India. Doctors and Patients Carry the Risk.

In healthcare, clinicians are taught that patient data protection is non-negotiable. One mistake can end a career. One chart left open can trigger discipline, fines, or worse.

But upstream, very different rules apply.

A recent investigation found that a major Medicaid contractor struggled to prevent live U.S. patient records from being accessed by offshore workers in India. These were not test environments or anonymized files. Employees described real systems, real patients, and repeated failed attempts to restrict access.

For clinicians, this creates an immediate imbalance.

Physicians are personally accountable for privacy violations they do not control. Documentation errors, access mistakes, or compliance lapses can lead to termination or licensure risk. Yet decisions to expose patient data are made far from the exam room, justified as “efficiency,” and insulated from the same consequences imposed on individual providers.

For institutions, the risk is far larger than most acknowledge.

Offshore access to protected health information carries substantial regulatory and contractual exposure. HIPAA penalties can reach millions of dollars per violation. State Medicaid contracts often include termination clauses, clawbacks, and liquidated damages. False Claims Act exposure can surface years later through audits or whistleblower actions, long after any short-term savings have been booked.

There are operational risks that receive far less scrutiny than clinical ones.

Offshoring models often involve high workforce turnover, layered subcontracting, and limited transparency into credential verification and access controls. Rapid churn increases insider risk and reduces auditability. These are not country-specific accusations. They are structural risks inherent to moving sensitive healthcare data outside the same enforcement and oversight frameworks used domestically.

There is also a quiet asymmetry in who bears the consequences.

Organizations that maintain strict data protections rarely see immediate financial reward. Instead, they may watch competitors cut costs by accepting risks they refuse to take. Enforcement is uneven. When it arrives, it is swift and devastating. Those who treated safeguards as flexible absorb fines, contract loss, and reputational damage that can threaten institutional survival. Those who did not take the risk remain standing.

For patients, the breach is often invisible until trust is gone.

Patients reasonably assume their medical information is handled under U.S. legal protections, by accountable parties, under enforceable standards. They are rarely informed when their data is accessed offshore, under different legal regimes. Even without a reported breach, that assumption, once broken, is difficult to restore.

This is not an isolated incident.

Healthcare systems routinely claim they lack funding for staffing, training, or expanded residency slots. At the same time, administrative and technical functions tied directly to patient data are offshored in the name of efficiency. Safeguards are described as robust, but treated as negotiable under financial pressure.

Healthcare is not interchangeable with other industries.

Patient data is not a commodity.
Efficiency is not neutral when it shifts risk onto clinicians, institutions, and patients who did not consent to carry it.
If offshore access to patient data continues without enforceable, auditable boundaries, a single regulatory action or contract finding can easily dwarf years of operational savings.

The lesson is simple.
Waiting for enforcement to force change is the most expensive way to learn.
